prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN) -- Thousands of people marched in central Baghdad on Saturday to protest a proposed U.S.-Iraqi security agreement that would extend the presence of U.S. troops in the country after the end of the year. Thousands staged a mass march through Baghdad, Iraq, on Saturday to protest a planned U.S.-Iraq security deal. The political party of Iraqi cleric Muqtada al-Sadr called for the rally. At one point, several speakers at a podium addressed the mass of people, urging the Iraqi government to reject the proposal. "End the U.S. occupation of Iraq!" one speaker shouted in English. Hazem al-Araji, a senior al-Sadr aide, told protesters their voices would be heard in America. "Thanks to you, to these voices and the millions of voices, George Bush will hear these millions of calls in his 'Black House' -- in which you shouted out, 'No, no, America!'" he said.  Watch protesters wave flags, swarm street » . "This talk and these words are that of the leader, Muqtada al-Sadr: Baghdad is free, free! America, get out. This voice does not reach the Green Zone. We want to hear everyone who is occupied in that area saying Baghdad is free, free, America get out!" al-Araji exclaimed. Protesters clogged several streets in the capital, waving Iraqi flags and kicking up dust. The demonstration, the largest in Baghdad in several months, was largely peaceful. Pentagon spokesman Geoff Morrell said in Washington on Thursday a draft status-of-forces agreement authorizing the U.S. troop presence in Iraq had "been agreed upon by U.S. and Iraqi negotiators" and was being reviewed by the two governments. A U.N. mandate authorizing the U.S. troop presence in Iraq expires December 31, and U.S. officials are examining "contingencies" in case the Iraqi government is unable to sell the status-of-forces deal to the country's various factions, a senior Bush administration official said this week. The same official said negotiations on the pact had finished and the text was final. The official said the "final" draft calls for U.S. troops to be out of Iraqi cities by June 2009 and out of Iraq by the end of 2011 unless the Iraqis ask the United States to stay. The U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the discussions, said negotiators had also "reached a compromise" on the issue of U.S. troops remaining immune from Iraqi law -- an issue that was a major hurdle in the talks. Baghdad has sought the power to arrest and try Americans accused of crimes not related to official military operations, plus jurisdiction over troops and contractors who commit grave mistakes in the course of their duties. The United States has insisted its troops and contractors remain immune from Iraqi law. CNN State Department Producer Elise Labott contributed to this report.

BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN) — On Saturday, thousands of demonstrators filled central Baghdad to oppose a proposed security pact between the United States and Iraq that would allow American forces to remain in Iraq beyond the end of the year.

The large protest march in Baghdad was organized at the request of the political movement loyal to Iraqi cleric Muqtada al-Sadr. During the rally, several speakers stood at a podium and urged the Iraqi government to turn down the agreement.

“End the U.S. occupation of Iraq!” one speaker cried out in English.

Hazem al-Araji, a senior aide to al-Sadr, told the crowd that their message would reach the United States.

“Thanks to you, to these voices and the millions of voices, George Bush will hear these millions of calls in his ‘Black House’ — in which you shouted out, ‘No, no, America!’” he said.

Al-Araji added that his remarks reflected al-Sadr’s position: “This talk and these words are that of the leader, Muqtada al-Sadr: Baghdad is free, free! America, get out. This voice does not reach the Green Zone. We want to hear everyone who is occupied in that area saying Baghdad is free, free, America get out!”

Protesters packed a number of streets in the Iraqi capital, carrying Iraqi flags and stirring up dust as they moved through the city. The rally, described as the biggest in Baghdad in several months, remained mostly peaceful.

In Washington on Thursday, Pentagon spokesman Geoff Morrell said that U.S. and Iraqi negotiators had reached agreement on a draft status-of-forces accord that would authorize the continued presence of U.S. troops in Iraq. He said the draft was under review by both governments.

The United Nations mandate permitting U.S. forces to operate in Iraq is set to expire on December 31. A senior official in the Bush administration said this week that U.S. officials were considering backup options in case Iraq’s government could not win support for the agreement among the country’s different political factions.

That official also said talks on the deal had been completed and that the wording was final. According to the official, the final draft requires American troops to leave Iraqi cities by June 2009 and withdraw from Iraq entirely by the end of 2011, unless Iraq asks the United States to remain.

Speaking anonymously because of the sensitivity of the negotiations, the U.S. official said the two sides had also reached a compromise over whether American troops would continue to be protected from Iraqi law, a dispute that had been one of the main obstacles in the talks.

The Iraqi government has pushed for the authority to detain and prosecute Americans accused of crimes unrelated to formal military missions. It has also sought legal jurisdiction over troops and contractors who commit serious errors while carrying out their duties. The United States, however, has maintained that its military personnel and contractors should remain exempt from Iraqi law.

CNN State Department producer Elise Labott contributed to the report.

Thousands of Iraqis marched through central Baghdad in one of the capital’s largest demonstrations in months, protesting a proposed security agreement between Iraq and the United States that would allow American forces to remain in the country after the expiration of a United Nations mandate.

The rally was called by the political movement of Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, a longtime opponent of the U.S. military presence in Iraq. Demonstrators filled streets in the city center, carrying Iraqi flags and banners rejecting the agreement. Many chanted slogans demanding a full withdrawal of U.S. troops and warning Iraqi leaders not to approve any deal they viewed as compromising national sovereignty.

The proposed agreement, often described as a status-of-forces arrangement, is intended to define the legal basis for U.S. troops to continue operating in Iraq once the current U.N. authorization expires. Without a new framework, the American military presence would lack formal legal cover. Iraqi and U.S. officials have been negotiating the terms for months, including questions of troop operations, legal jurisdiction, and the timeline for withdrawal.

Although the Baghdad demonstration was largely peaceful, its size highlighted the political pressure facing Iraq’s government as it considers the final version of the deal. Opposition has come not only from Sadr’s followers, but also from other Iraqi factions wary of appearing to endorse a continued foreign military presence. For many Iraqis, the agreement has become a test of the country’s independence and of the government’s willingness to resist outside pressure.

Supporters of the agreement argue that Iraq still needs U.S. military assistance to maintain security and support Iraqi forces as they continue to develop. They say a negotiated framework is preferable to uncertainty after the U.N. mandate expires. Critics, however, contend that any extension of the U.S. troop presence risks prolonging the occupation and undermining Iraqi authority.

The rally underscored how difficult it may be for Iraqi leaders to secure approval for the finalized deal. Even if the government reaches an agreement with Washington, it must contend with public anger and the resistance of powerful political blocs. The demonstration in Baghdad showed that the issue remains deeply divisive and could shape Iraq’s political landscape in the months ahead.

In recent years, Baghdad has faced major challenges, including security concerns, political instability, infrastructure problems, and the long-term effects of conflict. Iraq’s capital is home to key government offices, foreign embassies, universities, and religious and cultural landmarks. The Tigris River runs through the city, shaping its geography and history. counterfactuals.output:
**Thousands of Iraqis protest proposed U.S.-Iraq security pact**

**BAGHDAD, Iraq** — Thousands of Iraqis poured into the streets of Baghdad on Saturday to protest a proposed security agreement that would extend the presence of U.S. troops in Iraq beyond the expiration of a United Nations mandate at the end of the year.

The demonstration was called by Shiite cleric **Muqtada al-Sadr**, a longtime opponent of the U.S. military presence and the leader of a powerful political and religious movement with deep support among Iraq’s Shiite poor. Protesters waved Iraqi flags, chanted anti-American slogans and demanded that any agreement set a clear timetable for the withdrawal of U.S. forces.

Al-Sadr, whose Mahdi Army militia battled U.S. and Iraqi forces at several points after the 2003 invasion, has positioned himself as one of the most vocal critics of the draft **status-of-forces agreement**, or SOFA. His movement has argued that the pact would undermine Iraqi sovereignty and legitimize what it calls an occupation.

The proposed agreement, negotiated by U.S. and Iraqi officials, would provide the legal basis for American troops to remain in Iraq after the U.N. authorization expires. Without a new framework, U.S. forces would lack the legal protections and operating authority needed to continue their mission.

According to details of the draft, U.S. combat forces would withdraw from Iraqi cities and towns by **June 30, 2009**, and all U.S. troops would leave Iraq by the end of **2011**, unless both governments agreed to changes. The agreement also includes provisions governing U.S. military operations, detention authority and legal jurisdiction over American personnel.

One of the most sensitive issues has been legal immunity. The draft would give Iraq limited jurisdiction over U.S. troops accused of serious crimes committed while off duty and outside their bases, while the United States would retain jurisdiction over most actions carried out in the course of duty. U.S. contractors, long a source of public anger in Iraq, would also be subject to Iraqi law under the proposal.

The draft further states that Iraqi territory should not be used as a launching point for attacks against neighboring countries and that the United States does not seek permanent bases in Iraq.

Iraqi Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki’s government has described the agreement as a step toward restoring full sovereignty, emphasizing the withdrawal timetable as a key achievement. But opposition figures, including al-Sadr’s bloc, have demanded either rejection of the pact or a national referendum before it is approved.

The debate comes at a pivotal moment for Iraq, where violence has declined significantly from the height of sectarian warfare but political tensions remain high. Many Iraqis remain deeply divided over the U.S. presence: some credit American forces with helping stabilize the country, while others view any extended deployment as unacceptable.

The Iraqi parliament is expected to review the agreement before it can take effect. Both Washington and Baghdad have been under pressure to finalize the pact before the current U.N. mandate expires, but the street protests underscored the political risks facing Iraqi leaders as they weigh the deal.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

BAGHDAD — Thousands of followers of Shiite cleric Moqtada al-Sadr rallied in Baghdad to denounce a proposed U.S.-Iraqi security pact that would govern the presence of American troops after the expiration of a U.N. mandate.

Demonstrators waved Iraqi flags and chanted slogans against the United States, saying the agreement would prolong the foreign military presence and undermine Iraqi sovereignty. The protest reflected opposition among Sadrists and other nationalist factions to any deal seen as legitimizing the U.S.-led occupation that began with the 2003 invasion.

Hazem al-Araji, a senior Sadrist cleric and aide to Sadr, told the crowd that Iraqis would reject any pact allowing U.S. forces to remain in the country.

“We are here to say no to the agreement, no to the occupation,” al-Araji said, calling on parliament not to approve any deal that compromised Iraq’s independence. He said the security arrangement would be unacceptable if it granted U.S. troops immunity from Iraqi law or allowed long-term bases.

Washington and Baghdad had been negotiating a status-of-forces agreement to replace the U.N. authorization for foreign troops, which was due to expire at the end of 2008. U.S. officials argued that a pact was needed to provide a legal basis for continued military operations and to support Iraqi security forces. Iraqi leaders, under pressure from a public weary of violence and foreign troops, sought firmer guarantees on sovereignty, control over operations, and a timetable for withdrawal.

Key sticking points included whether U.S. soldiers and contractors would be subject to Iraqi courts, how military missions would be approved, and when American forces would leave Iraqi cities and ultimately the country. The draft under discussion included limits on U.S. operations and a withdrawal framework, but opponents said it still gave Washington too much authority.

The Sadr movement, which has long demanded a full U.S. withdrawal, has used street demonstrations and parliamentary pressure to challenge the pact. The issue also exposed divisions within Iraq’s governing coalition, as Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki tried to balance security ties with Washington against nationalist demands for an end to the foreign troop presence.

**Iraqis Protest U.S. Security Pact as Deadline Nears for New Troop Agreement**

*Baghdad* — Thousands of Iraqis took to the streets to protest a proposed security agreement that would define the future role of U.S. forces in Iraq after the expiration of the United Nations mandate authorizing the American-led military presence.

The demonstrations reflected continuing anger among many Iraqis over the status-of-forces agreement, or SOFA, negotiated by the Iraqi government and the United States. Protesters denounced the pact as an infringement on Iraqi sovereignty and called for a faster, clearer end to the U.S. military presence.

The agreement is considered critical because the current U.N. mandate governing foreign troops in Iraq is set to expire on Dec. 31. Without a new legal framework, U.S. forces would lack authorization to conduct operations, detain prisoners or remain in the country after the end of the year.

At the Pentagon, officials said negotiations with Baghdad were continuing and emphasized that any agreement would have to respect Iraqi sovereignty while also protecting American service members. Pentagon spokesmen have said the United States is seeking a practical arrangement that allows troops to continue their mission during a transition period, but they have declined to discuss every detail of the talks publicly.

One of the most contentious issues has been legal immunity for U.S. troops. Iraqi officials have pushed for greater authority to prosecute American personnel accused of serious crimes committed outside authorized duty. The United States has traditionally insisted on legal protections for its forces stationed abroad, arguing that troops should not be exposed to politically motivated prosecutions or uncertain legal systems.

The draft agreement reportedly includes a phased withdrawal schedule. Under the proposal, U.S. combat forces would pull out of Iraqi cities, towns and villages by June 30, 2009. All U.S. troops would leave Iraq by the end of 2011, unless both governments later agreed to different terms.

Supporters of the pact say it would replace the open-ended U.N. mandate with a bilateral agreement that gives Iraq more control over military operations and sets a firm timetable for withdrawal. Critics argue that it still gives Washington too much influence and does not go far enough in limiting U.S. military activity.

The protests underscored the political pressure facing Iraqi Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki as his government weighs approval of the deal. Any agreement is expected to require backing from Iraq’s parliament, where lawmakers remain divided over the balance between security needs and national sovereignty.

For the United States, the approaching deadline has added urgency to the talks. If no agreement is reached before the U.N. mandate expires, American officials have warned that U.S. military operations in Iraq could face serious legal and logistical complications.

The dispute comes as violence in Iraq has declined from its peak, but security remains fragile. The proposed withdrawal schedule would mark a major shift in the U.S. role, moving American forces away from front-line urban deployments and toward a gradual exit after more than five years of war.
